# Getting started

Prospektor is a workspace where a sales team researches target
companies and drafts partner pitches. You type a company; the studio works
out who that company actually is from its own website, researches it, scores
partnership fit against what your workspace says it is hunting for, and
drafts your enabled deliverables — pitch deck, one-pager, cold-email
sequence, written proposal — plus a decision-maker list and lookalike
companies to pitch next.

## Before you have an account — the free run

You do not need a workspace, a card or even an email address to see what
Prospektor finds. A **free run** lives at `/r` on the studio: type any company
website — or just their name — and the studio does the first half of its job in
front of you.

1. **It reads the site** — what that company sells and to whom, and two or
   three things visibly true from their own pages. Where we can confirm them,
   the first facts on the strip are checked against a company database rather
   than read off the page: headcount, location, industry. It says so underneath, and
   it counts: *"Read just now: 1 page and 2 web searches of acme.com."* If it
   ever says *"nothing here was opened just now"* instead, that is the studio
   telling you the truth rather than dressing a guess up as a reading — check
   what it says about you and correct the next step if it is off.
2. **It says what it thinks you should be hunting for** — one sentence naming
   the kind of company worth approaching. This is a guess, and it is meant to
   be corrected: *"That's not it — let me say"* opens a box, and one line in
   your own words ("agencies that resell hosting", "family offices in the
   Nordics") sends it looking for those instead.
3. **It finds real companies** — three of them, each with its own website, two
   or three checkable facts, a fit score on the same 0–100 scale a paid run
   uses, and one sentence on why this company.

Then, if you want it, one more thing: **who you are up against**. *Name a
competitor* takes one rival's website and reads them the way it read you — what
they sell, how they position themselves, our read of what they actually do, who
they sell to, and **a list of their clients with the page that names each one**.
Their clients are your prospect list, which is why that list is the point of the
block rather than a footnote. One rival per free run.

One line of that report is deliberately blank. *How you win* is the only line a
competitor's own website could never answer, because it comes from your brief —
so the free version says it needs one instead of guessing at a slogan. A
workspace writes it.

Then it stops. What a free run gives you is **who to approach**. What a
workspace gives you is **what to send them** — the pitch in your own voice, the
deliverables, the decision-makers, the prep sheet, and a source behind every
claim. That is the line, and the free run says so on the page rather than
springing it on you.

Every free run has its own address, `/r/<token>`, and it keeps working. Send
it to a colleague and they see the whole thing — they are not asked to sign in,
because there is nothing to sign in to. Nothing about a free run is listed,
indexed or searchable: the link is the only way to it, so it is as private as
whoever you send it to.

**If you would rather not lose it, we will send it to you.** *While you wait*
appears under the steps as the run works, and again at the bottom of a finished
run: an email address and a mobile number, both needed to have the run sent.
The run does not wait for either — the companies appear whether you fill this
in or not, and the link in your address bar works either way.

Under those fields there is one box, *Product news and tips, by email and text*,
and it starts **ticked**. Untick it and nothing at all is kept: no list, no
record, and the number you typed is not stored — you get the link and that is
the end of it. Leave it ticked and you get the same news a customer gets, a few
times a month at most, by email and sometimes by text, and every one of those
emails carries a one-click unsubscribe that works without signing in to
anything. It is the same permission the studio asks for on your first day with
an account, so if you later buy a workspace you will not be asked twice, and you
can change it any time in [Your account](/settings/account) → *How we may reach
you*.

Your number is held the way an account's is: in full international form, one per
person, and a number you have already set on an account is never replaced by one
typed here. Deleting your data deletes it with everything else — see
[Privacy](/help/privacy).

### "Why did I get an email about a run I did weeks ago?"

If you ran a free run, left that box ticked and never opened a workspace, you
may get **one** email pointing you back at your own run. One, ever — not a
sequence, and there is no second one waiting behind it. It links to your
`/r/<token>` and to nothing else, so it opens without signing in, the same way
it did the day you ran it.

The unsubscribe link on it stops that email **and** the product news it was sent
on: they are the same permission, so one click ends both. If you have already
opened a workspace you are not on the list at all, and if you unticked the box
there is no record of you to be on it.

A free run is genuinely free and it is capped for the day as a whole, so
occasionally it will ask you to come back tomorrow. A company somebody has
already run comes back instantly and costs nothing — and the same is true of
competitor reports, which have a smaller daily cap of their own because they are
a much bigger piece of work.

## The free workspace — one full pitch

Signing up gets you a workspace of your own, and everything a paid one does
right up to the second run.

If you came from a free run and corrected what it said you were hunting for,
that sentence comes with you: the studio opens your brief on your words instead
of asking you the question again. Correct it there any time — **Your brief**
shows whose sentence it is.

You answer the onboarding, the studio reads your site and writes your brief,
and **For you** fills with real companies it thinks you should approach. Press
**Prospekt** on one and you get the whole thing: the research, the fit case,
who decides, and every deliverable your workspace has switched on — written in
your voice, with a source behind each claim.

That is the one run. After it, `/upgrade` is what you meet when you press the
next one.

**Nothing is taken away.** Your brief, your pitch, your library and the rest of
the leads on **For you** stay exactly where they are, readable and shareable.
What stops is starting the next run — a second pitch, a glance, a competitor
report, a call prep sheet, an inbound judgment, warm paths, a rescan. A
subscription starts them again immediately, on the same workspace, with the
work already in it.

The competitor report that stops is the one written **from your brief** — your
read, your suppress list, a Prospekt button on each of their clients, and *How
you win* filled in. The neutral version at a free run is still free to anyone,
and still leaves that line blank.

Two things worth knowing. The **one run belongs to the workspace, not to you**,
so a free account holds one workspace — being invited into a colleague's
changes nothing. And **asking what a run would cost is always free**, whether
or not you have spent yours.

## Your first minutes

- **Sign-in** is Google, a passkey, or an emailed link — there are no
  passwords. Access is your workspace's email allowlist; if your address is
  on it, you are in. Adding a **passkey** takes one press in
  [Your account](/settings/account), and after that signing in
  is Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello or a security key, with nothing to type
  and no link to wait for. See *Signing in* below.
- **Value first, account chores last.** The first time you sign in, the
  studio leads with the work: if it has already found your first three
  companies, they are the first thing you see, and the guided tour follows
  (or skip straight to the dashboard). What the account still needs — a
  **recovery phone number** (so we can get you back in if you lose access to
  your email), **how we may reach you** (all optional, all off unless you
  tick them), and, if nobody here has confirmed it yet, **what your company
  is called** — waits as one quiet *Complete your account info* line on the
  dashboard, and can always be answered later in
  [Your account](/settings/account).
- **One question comes before your company name: whose studio this is** —
  *My own company*, or *A client of mine*. An agency picking the second gets
  the five questions below asked about their client rather than about them,
  deliverables written as the client and never mentioning the agency, and a
  workspace name somebody is still asked to confirm. Leave both alone and it
  reads as your own, which is what it always did. Change it any time in
  [Workspace settings](/settings/workspace) → *Whose studio this is*.
- A brand-new workspace opens with a **first draft**, not with a question. The
  studio reads your own website and leads with the two things that are work
  rather than facts about you: who it would go and find, and the paragraph it
  would open with in your voice. **What else we read** opens the rest — what it
  read off your site, where it would look, who you are up against, and what it
  would score those companies against. Every block says where its text came
  from — our guess from your site, or your own words — and a block only you can
  fill stays empty rather than being filled in with something plausible. Where
  somebody has already scanned your domain, the draft starts from confirmed
  company data — industry, headcount, founding year — instead of guessing at it.
  Where you *sell* is never guessed from where you are registered: it stays
  empty until you say.
- **A workspace an agency made for you skips the draft and the questions.** You
  land in the studio itself, on the suggested leads. The agency answers those
  questions on your behalf when it creates the workspace, and either of you can
  finish them any time from [Your brief](/settings/brief).
- **Then one question: what first?** The draft is followed by a fork — three
  doors, with *Companies to pitch* already chosen, and **Continue** the only
  button, so the usual act is a single press. The other two doors are
  *a competitor's clients* (name one rival, get the list of who they sell to)
  and *lookalikes of your customers* (name two, get companies like them). Take
  either of those and you are in front of that question straight away instead
  of behind five others — nothing is lost, because the door you skipped is
  still there afterwards: your three suggested companies still arrive,
  [Counterprospekt](/competitors) still takes a competitor's name, and
  **Lookalikes** stands on the home screen for good. The five questions move
  behind the door, onto [Your brief](/settings/brief).
- Underneath it is a short **interview** — five questions: what to hunt for,
  **where and how big**, **a few competitors by name**, **a few customers and
  why they are good ones**, how you want to sound. Each screen is one calm question and the
  field that answers it, nothing else — and each answer sharpens that draft
  and every future pitch: your sentence replaces our guess in the brief. They
  are asked while the studio researches your company in the background, every
  one of them is answerable from the first second, and you can skip all five
  and come back via [Your brief](/settings/brief) — **Take me in** works
  from every screen, and your workspace already exists behind it.

### The example pitch in your library

Your [Library](/library) is not empty on day one. There is one pitch in it
already, labelled **Example**, and it is there so you can read a finished run
while your own are still going — your three take a few minutes each, and the
example takes none.

- **It is invented, and identical in every workspace.** Harborline Freight and
  Ledgerpost are both made up. Nothing in it was researched, and its 94 is the
  example's own score, not a judgment the studio made about anything of yours.
- **It shows the real screen.** The fit thesis, the deck, the cold email
  sequence, the one-pager, the proposal, the decision-makers and the lookalikes
  are laid out exactly where your own runs put them.
- **It is read-only.** No pencil, no share link, no call prep, and its
  lookalikes cannot be run — it is an illustration, so it never touches your
  brief, your voice or your outcomes.
- **Remove** takes it away in one press and it stays away on this device, and
  it goes on its own as soon as your first real pitch lands.

### Name a few customers, and why they are good ones

The fourth question is the highest-value thirty seconds in the interview, and
the **why** is the reason.

- **Two or three is plenty; five is better.** One per line: the company, then
  what makes that one good. *"Northwind — their CFO had the same problem"* is a
  complete answer.
- **Real ones, or the ones you wish you had.** A workspace on day one has no
  wins to name and the question still works — a dream customer with a reason is
  as useful as a closed one.
- **The names alone are not the point.** Anyone can find companies that look
  like a list of names. What the studio cannot guess is *why* those are the good
  ones, and that reason becomes the thesis every prospect is scored against.
- **What you want more of** sits beside it, with two one-tap suggestions.
  *More companies like these* keeps the studio close to what already works;
  *Adjacent markets, related to these* treats your customers as a starting point
  and looks for the neighbouring category your strengths carry into. It is a box
  rather than a switch, so *"mostly more like these, but I want to test
  facilities management"* is a real answer.

Both are on [Who we hunt](/settings/hunt) afterwards, and editable there.

### Where should we hunt, and how big?

The second question is two plain boxes with one-tap suggestions under each, and
it is worth thirty seconds because everything the studio does afterwards reads
it — which companies are suggested to you, which ones a run goes looking for,
and how each is scored.

- **Geography** arrives pre-filled with our guess from your own site. Write
  over it in whatever words you like: `Germany`, `English-speaking countries`,
  `DACH`, `the Nordics plus the Netherlands`, or `Anywhere`. There is no list
  to pick from, on purpose — most real answers are not a country.
- **Company size** starts empty, because nothing on your website says what size
  of company *you* want to approach. `Mid-market and enterprise`, `startups
  under 50`, `exclude solopreneurs` are all fine answers, as is leaving it
  blank.
- Taps add up: a second suggestion joins the first (`Mid-market (51–500),
  Enterprise (500+)`), and tapping a lit one removes it.
- Both are **preferences, not filters.** A strong company just outside your
  stated area is still shown to you, and the pitch says plainly that it sits
  outside it — so the call stays yours. If you mean something absolute, say so
  in the box (`only Germany`, `never outside the EU`) and it is read that way.
- Answering the geography also makes web searches run from your own country
  where you named exactly one, so results come back the way they would for
  somebody sitting there rather than from a default locale.
- Change either at any time in [Your brief](/settings/brief), under the
  questions. Both appear as **Where you hunt** in [Workspace
  settings](/settings/workspace) → *Workspace configuration*, and the next run
  uses the new answer.

### Name a few competitors

The third question asks who you are up against — two or three names are
plenty, in whatever words you like, and it is skippable like everything else.
The studio never guesses your rivals off your site, so anything in this answer
is yours. It reads the names as a **map of your market**: suggestions hunt the
territory around them — companies that partner with those names, sell alongside
them, or serve the same buyers — and are told plainly that a company you
compete with is not one to suggest to you. The names also arrive on
[Counterprospekt](/competitors) as chips, where one tap runs that competitor's
report — answer in whatever words you like, *"acme.com as well as
fieldlens.io"* becomes two chips, not one. Change or add names any time in
[Your brief](/settings/brief); the deeper question there — *who do you lose
to, and why do you win* — is separate, and sharpens how pitches answer the
objection rather than whom the studio targets.
- The **guided tour** opens on your first landing and walks the example pitch a
  deliverable at a time — fit thesis, deck, cold email, decision-makers,
  lookalikes — with its card and a ring travelling to the block each step is
  about, and it ends back on the home screen at the tile that starts a run of
  your own. You can bring it back by unticking "Do not show this again" on its
  last step next time it shows, and skipping it never loses anything.
- The home screen, [Leads](/), proposes companies worth pitching next,
  one card at a time — a thumbs-up starts a real pitch immediately. Each card's
  facts are read off that company's own website, which the studio opens while it
  is looking, rather than off a search result about them — so they are checkable
  by anyone who opens the same page. A card with only two facts on it is the
  studio declining to pad; a company it could not stand up at all is left off.
  A card leaves the shelf when you remove it, glance it or run it — including
  when you run that company from [New pitch](/pitch/new) instead, so the shelf
  never offers work you have already done. To remove one, press the **×** on
  the card and say which kind it is: **Not a fit**, or **Our client**. A card
  naming a company you already sell to is good news — the studio found your
  customers — and *Our client* puts it on your [suppress list](/suppress) as
  a customer, onto [Who we hunt](/settings/hunt) as one, and the next search
  hunts for more like it. Anything you glanced is in
  [Library](/library), where you can reopen it. The search for the next few starts the moment
  your first cards are handed to you, not once you have spent them, so there
  is normally something waiting by the time you come back. While the shelf is
  empty it says what of yours is running and links you to it.
- **A weak fit is never suggested.** The score on a card is out of 100 —
  75 and up is a strong fit, 50 and up promising — and anything the search
  would score under 50 is held back rather than shown. You will see two cards,
  or one, or none, before you see a 42: a shelf that pads itself with a
  company nobody should call is a shelf you stop reading. When that leaves
  nothing to show, the screen says how many were held back and asks for the
  two answers that sharpen the next search most — **who already buys from
  you** and **who you compete with**, both on
  [Who we hunt](/settings/hunt).
- **The shelf learns from what you press.** A company you glance at and then
  research in full is the clearest thing you can tell the studio about what you
  want — clearer than your brief, because you looked and then you spent. From
  the second one of those, the next search hunts for that shape. It fades:
  a press stops counting after three months, so a curious click in week one
  does not steer you for ever. And one card a search is a deliberate bet
  *outside* that shape, marked **Adjacent bet** on the tile — a shelf that only
  ever returns what you already pressed on narrows onto one kind of company and
  stops being worth opening. Where you have said which way to hunt on
  [Who we hunt](/settings/hunt), or typed what you are after, that decides
  instead and the studio does not second-guess it.
- **Five companies to rate, before the deck lets you go.** Three cards in,
  the studio puts up five companies and asks one thing about each: would you
  go after them? None of them is a lead and none is being offered — they are
  chosen to be *different from each other*, one squarely what you asked for
  and the rest a size up, a sector across, a country over, a different way of
  selling. Your noes are the point. Most people cannot write down what a good
  lead looks like and everybody can recognise one, so five taps say more than
  a sixth interview question would. What the answers show is written into
  *What you have corrected us on* on [Who we hunt](/settings/hunt), where
  every later search reads it and a cross takes any line back off. Answers
  that show no pattern teach nothing, and the studio says so rather than
  inventing a rule. *Skip* goes straight past it; the set is offered once.
- **The deck ends on one question: who do you lose deals to?** It is the same
  door the fork offers first — reached from the deck if you took the default,
  and reached in one press if you did not. Name one and
  the studio reads their site and lists their clients — that list is your
  prospect list, and it lands in
  [Counterprospekt](/competitors). The box arrives carrying a competitor your
  brief already names, so the usual act is one press rather than one more
  question, and the name you give is written into your brief exactly as the
  interview's third question would have written it. *Skip* goes straight to
  the studio and nothing is lost — [Counterprospekt](/competitors) takes a
  competitor's name any time.
- **Lookalikes** is the other half of that idea, and it stands on the home
  screen for good: name customers you already have and the studio finds more
  companies like them. The tile sits beside *Custom pitch*; the box arrives
  carrying the customers you named at onboarding, so the usual act is one
  press. What comes back lands on [For you](/leads) as ordinary cards — glance one for
  fifteen seconds to see the roles worth approaching, or run the full pitch.
  Adding *"— why they are a good one"* after a name tells the search which way
  to be alike; a name it has not heard before is written into your brief, and
  the reasons you gave at onboarding are never overwritten.
- **Getting started** (`/start`) is where signing in lands you, and it is the
  first entry in the sidebar. It has two steps.

  **Step 1, Customize your studio** — the three things that make every later
  pitch better: run a pitch, fix a line you would never send, and say what
  happened. Only the step you are on shows its button; the other two are a line
  each, so there is one thing to do rather than three. The number beside the
  sidebar entry is how many are left, and it goes when none are.

  **Step 2, What can we prospekt for you today?** — seven cards, one press each:
  companies to pitch, one company you name, a competitor's clients, lookalikes
  of your customers, who to contact, a warm introduction, and a sheet before a
  call. Once step 1 is finished it disappears — its three acts have permanent
  homes in the sidebar under *For you*, *Library* and *What happened* — and the
  seven cards become the whole screen, with one of them recommended.

  The one-minute tour lives at the foot of that page, so it is always somewhere
  to go back to.
- Stuck at any point? **Support**, at the foot of the sidebar, opens a chat
  that answers in seconds and remembers where you left off; its
  **💡 Request a feature** toggle sends an idea, an improvement or a bug
  report straight to the Prospektor team.

## The core loop

1. Open [New pitch](/pitch/new), enter a company name or domain (the field
   autocompletes and warns if your team already pitched them). Every box in the
   studio that takes a company name does the same — the [outcome
   editor](/outcomes), [Counterprospekt](/counter), the [suppress
   list](/suppress), a new client workspace — and picking a suggestion fills
   the website box beside it.
2. The run takes minutes and shows six live stages — understand, research,
   score, draft, people, check. You can leave any time: runs continue in the
   background and are listed under [Running](/running).
3. The finished pitch lands in the [Library](/library): summary, fit thesis,
   signals for and against, deliverables, decision-makers, lookalikes.
4. Edit any deliverable in place (the pencil). Saved edits teach the studio
   your team's voice — tone only, never facts — so future pitches sound more
   like you.
5. Record what happened on the card itself — press the badge, pick what
   happened. Closed deals feed the Leads shelf, so what it offers drifts
   toward what actually closes — and under those, the glances you paid to
   research in full.

## This documentation

Everything the Support chat knows lives in these pages, and they are also
published at [prospektor.ai/help](https://prospektor.ai/help) — searchable,
and always describing the version of the studio that is actually running.

## Pointing an AI assistant at Prospektor

[studio.prospektor.ai/llms.txt](https://studio.prospektor.ai/llms.txt) is the
door an agent reads: what Prospektor is, and the handful of calls it can make
without an account — a first look at any domain, what that look would cost, and
this whole documentation corpus as JSON.

There are no API keys yet, so an assistant cannot open your workspace, read your
briefs or start a pitch on your behalf. Everything in a workspace still needs a
person signed in.

## Signing in

There are three ways in, and they all check the same access list.

**A passkey** is the fastest and the safest. Add one from
[Your account](/settings/account) → *Add a passkey* while you are
signed in; your device makes a key, keeps the secret half where it can never
leave, and hands us only the public half. After that, going to the studio and
touching your fingerprint sensor is the whole sign-in — most browsers offer the
passkey in the email field's own drop-down before you press anything, and
there is a **Sign in with a passkey** button underneath *Continue with Google*
for the ones that do not.

A passkey only works on this site. That is not a limitation, it is the point: a
convincing copy of our sign-in page cannot ask your device for it, so there is
nothing for anyone to phish out of you.

You can add one on each device you use, see them all in *Your account*, and
remove any of them there. Removing a passkey stops it opening the studio; the
key your device still holds simply opens nothing.

**Google** is the front door for anyone with a Google account, and it is the
only door besides a passkey that can carry Prospektor's own operator role.

**An emailed link** is the fallback for an address that cannot use Google. It
works once and expires after 15 minutes, and your access is checked when you
click it rather than when it was sent.

## Your recovery phone number

We ask for it once — behind the *Complete your account info* line on the
dashboard, after your first leads and the tour, never in front of them — and
you can skip it. It is there so
that if you lose access to your email — the thing every other way in depends on
— there is still a way to get you back into an account you are paying for, and
so there is a way to reach you about the account itself.

Pick your country from the dropdown first, then write the number the way you
normally would: `0176 1234567` under Germany, `415 555 0134` under the United
States. Both become the same international number underneath. If you would
rather type the whole thing with a `+` in front, that works too and overrides
the dropdown.

It is used for nothing else unless you say so on the next question. It is never
sent to a model, never appears in a pitch, a proposal or a shared link, and is
never used for marketing without your say-so. Change it or clear it any time in
[Your account](/settings/account).

## How we may reach you

The same card asks which ways of contacting you are all right. Four separate
questions, **all off unless you turn them on**:

- **Product news and tips, by email** — what shipped and what other teams get
  out of it, a few times a month at most.
- **Text me about my account** — security alerts, and help getting back in.
- **Product news, by text** — the same news as the email, if a text suits you
  better.
- **You may call me** — about your account, or to ask what would make
  Prospektor more useful to you.

They are four questions rather than one on purpose: wanting a security text is
not the same as wanting a marketing one, and you should not have to take both
to get either.

If you bought your workspace on prospektor.ai, the payment step there carries
the same unticked *Product news and tips, by email* box. A tick given at
checkout is recorded against your address before you first sign in, so you are
not asked twice — and it is undone the same way as any other answer, in
[Your account](/settings/account) → *How we may reach you* or by
the one-click unsubscribe on any such email.

**Account email is not on that list, because it is not optional.** Sign-in
links, receipts and service notices come with having an account — there is no
way to turn those off and still have one.

Today none of these actually send anything: Prospektor has no mailing list, no
text-message provider and nobody making calls. We ask now because you are
already filling in a form, and turning any of them on or off later is one click
in [Your account](/settings/account).

## The getting-started course — eight emails, one a day

Once it is switched on, a new workspace's members get one short email a day for
eight days, each teaching one thing the studio does, in the order you meet
them: where you land, the companies under **For you**, what one Prospekt
gives you, the edit that teaches the studio your voice, saying what happened,
importing your network, warm paths, and letting your own tools call the
workspace. Each is a few lines and one link.

It is not the *product news* box above and does not need it: it goes to you
because you have a workspace, the way a *your run is ready* email does. **One
click on any lesson stops the rest**, without signing in, and a stopped course
does not restart. Sign-in links and emails about your own work are unaffected.

## What your company is called

Your workspace's name goes on every brief, pitch and shared link it produces —
so if it was created from a checkout field, by an agency, or from an uploaded
list, the first owner or admin to sign in is asked to confirm it reads the way
you would write it. Changing it there rewrites your brief, which is what every
pitch is composed from.

If you made the workspace yourself by typing your company name, nobody asks you
again — you already answered.

Once it has been answered, it holds. The studio reads your site again in the
background — when the first research lands, and every time you accept a rescan
months later — and it forms its own opinion about what your company is called
from the way your marketing pages write it. That opinion never overrules yours:
whoever confirmed the name is the last word on it, and a later reading can
change everything else in your brief without touching it. On a workspace nobody
has confirmed yet, the studio's reading is still the better answer and does
replace the name the checkout or the uploaded list came with.

## Your setup call

Getting your brief right is the one thing everything else runs on — the fit
scores, the research, the drafts, the shared links. So on your first arrival at
the front door you are offered **a call to set it up with you**. It is included
in what you already pay, it takes about half an hour, and it is the fastest
route to a pitch you would actually send.

Press **Book a time** on the account card and your own calendar opens on a real
person's availability. If you would rather get on with it, take *Skip for now*:
the offer waits a few days and then asks once more, and it stops asking as soon
as you have saved your first deliverable — at that point you got where the call
was for.

You can ask for one at any time afterwards from the support panel — the same
place you ask a question or request a feature — under **Book a setup call**.
That door does not close when you skip the card, and it does not close once
your workspace is working: a call is worth having whenever you are stuck.

What we record is that the offer was made and what you did with it — a
timestamp, no more. The calendar itself belongs to whoever you booked with; the
studio never sees who else is on it or what is in your diary.

If your studio shows no such offer, this deploy has no calendar attached to it
yet, and there is nothing to book.

# The screens, and where each one lives

Every screen has a real URL. When pointing someone somewhere, use these
exact paths.

| Screen | Path | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| For you | `/leads` | Companies the studio proposes pitching next, one card at a time, plus tiles for Call prep and Inbound prospecting |
| A warm introduction | `/intro` | Two directions, and you pick one. **Someone to introduce me** — name a company, and the studio maps your network against them: who could open the door, why, the tie verified against a page it read, and two drafts for the best path (the ask you send your contact, and the finished email for them to send on). **Someone worth meeting, for a contact** — name somebody you already know, and it says who else in your network they should meet, what each side gets, and a double opt-in note. If you have not brought in your network yet, the screen asks for that first and nothing else: an introduction runs through somebody you know, so there is nothing to search until it is there |
| Lookalikes | `/lookalikes` | Name customers you already have; the studio finds more companies like them and puts them on For you |
| Your agents | `/agents` | Describe what you want done, in one sentence, and the studio builds the agent that does it. It picks the door — find leads, lookalikes, a glance, a pitch, decision-makers, a competitor report, or a standing watch on one rival — and fills in what that door needs from your brief. A watch reports what that company publicly did since the last look, each move dated, sourced, and with one line on what to do about it. The agent is kept, so next time it is one press — and a sentence that says how often ("every Monday") makes it standing, running itself until you press Stop. When a sentence names something the studio cannot do yet, it says so instead of doing the nearest thing |
| New pitch | `/pitch/new` | The form: company name or domain, optional contact, motion and value angle from your workspace's own vocabulary; ⚡ Beast Mode at its foot for a whole list |
| Running | `/running` | Runs in flight; Watch drops into the live terminal; a stuck run can be dismissed, a live one stopped |
| Getting started (home) | `/start` | Where signing in lands you. **Step 1, Customize your studio** — run a pitch, fix a line you would never send, say what happened. Only the step you are on shows its button; the others are a line each, and the number in the sidebar is how many are left. **Step 2, What can we prospekt for you today?** — six cards, one press each: companies to pitch, one company you name, a competitor's clients, lookalikes of your customers, who to contact, and a sheet before a call. Once step 1 is done it goes away and the six cards are the whole screen, with one of them recommended. The one-minute tour is at the foot |
| Library | `/library` | Saved pitches as cards, sortable, with unread markers; press a card to open it, its badge to record what happened, and its ⋯ menu for Call prep |
| A pitch | `/pitches/<id>` | One run — live while it works, the finished pitch after |
| What happened | `/outcomes` | The full history for every prospect — notes, the timeline, and "Make sense of this", which reads a record back. On the sidebar under **Teach Prospektor**, because what you record here is what every later pitch is written from. Recording an outcome does not need this screen: that is a press on the lead itself |
| Counterprospekt | `/competitors` | Opens on the companies we think compete for your customers, each with the one line saying why and one press to research them properly. Under that: name a competitor yourself, then the reports you have run and where you stand across all of them, then the first page of search results for what your buyers type and where you sit on it. The two lists differ on purpose — search finds who a buyer meets, the top block finds who competes for the same deal, and a company can be one without being the other. A report gives what they sell, how they position themselves, who they sell to, and a sourced list of their clients — each client a one-press pitch of your own |
| A competitor report | `/competitors/<id>` | One report — live while it researches, the finished report after. Three lines that take your side (their strength · their weakness · how we win), four cards of three bullets each (they sell · their positioning · their customers · our read), then their clients as your prospect list; re-run it any time, or remove a company that turned out not to be a competitor |
| Call prep | `/prep` | One sheet for a specific upcoming call — goal, framing, talking points, the likely objection with an answer |
| Evaluate inbound | `/evaluate` | Paste outreach somebody sent you, get an honest take-the-call-or-skip-it with reasons |
| Your network | `/network` | Import who the team knows (LinkedIn export or pasted list) — the raw material for warm paths |
| Suppress list | `/suppress` | The brief’s second tab: companies and people this workspace will never approach, plus the standing rules that rule out the rest |
| Who we hunt | `/settings/hunt` | Everything that decides which companies reach you: what you are looking for, where and how big, the market around you, what you have told the studio to keep looking for, what you have corrected it on, and what it must never bring back |
| Your brief | `/settings/brief` | The brief every deliverable is written from — facts, voice, guardrails, banned terms — with one question to answer beneath it, and the rest folded at the foot |
| Your account | `/settings/account` | Yours rather than the workspace's: passkeys, recovery phone, which emails the studio sends you and how else it may reach you |
| Workspace settings | `/settings/workspace` | Six cards, nothing folded: **Workspace** (name, website, whose studio this is), **Access** (who can sign in, and your own role), **Brand** (colours, then the deliverable stylesheet), **Sharing** (every link the team has sent, and Revoke), **Plan** (pause or cancel) and **Danger zone**. The old `/shares` address opens it |
| Upgrade | `/upgrade` | Free workspaces only: what your one full pitch bought, and the way to the rest of your list. Your brief, pitch and leads stay readable behind it |
| Who opens which door | `/paths` | Agencies only: one console across every client workspace you hold. It reads **your** network against every company those workspaces are working on — their suggestions as well as their finished pitches — and ranks the doors, best first. Somebody who works at the company beats somebody whose note mentions it, whatever else you know about them. Free to open and no research runs: pressing a row switches you into that client's workspace and opens the introduction ask there, so the drafts come out in their voice. Reached from **Your network** |
| Portfolio uploads | `/portfolio` | Agencies only: how your last portfolio upload is going, and the ones before it |

The sidebar carries fourteen of them: **Getting started** on its own at the
top, then **Leads** (For you, New pitch, Your agents, Running, Library,
Counterprospekt), **Meetings** (Call prep, Evaluate inbound) and **Teach
Prospektor** (Who we hunt, Your brief, Your network, What happened, Settings).
**Your account** is in the workspace menu at the sidebar's head, not on the
sidebar — those settings are yours and follow you into every workspace you
belong to.

Three screens are reached from inside another rather than from the sidebar,
because that is where you are when you want them. **Lookalikes** is a card on
Getting started, and a tile on For you beside Custom pitch. The **Suppress
list** is the second tab on Your brief — the brief says what this workspace
hunts for and the suppress list says what it never hunts. **Sharing** is a card
on Settings.

**Who opens which door** reads only the workspaces you can already open. It is
your own memberships intersected with the workspaces you created — so a client
who has since removed you, or one you detached, is not on it. It maps your
network **down** to their companies and never reads their network back up.

**A warm introduction** used to be a panel you could only reach on a finished
pitch. It still appears there — a pitch you have already run shows its paths
without being asked — but the screen above is the way in when you have not run
one, and it is the only place the second direction lives.

**Who to contact** is the one card that borrows a screen. It opens New pitch
with one line saying what the press will do, and the button reads *Find the
people* rather than *Glance* — same field, different verb. Coming to New pitch
any other way gives you the ordinary form back.

Three old addresses still work: `/` opens Getting started, `/settings` opens
Your brief, and `/shares` opens Settings.

**Counterprospekt** deserves one more sentence, because its rule is strict:
a report names a company as the competitor's client **only when a page the
run actually read says so**, and every entry links that page. A claimed
client without a source is left out and counted, never shown. The competitors
you named at onboarding sit under the box as chips — one tap runs that report,
and the box is for anyone else. Finished
reports also appear in the Library, and a company on your suppress list can
still be analyzed — the list says who not to *approach*, so a suppressed
company in their client list simply gets no pitch button.

### What a report says

A finished report opens on **three lines that take your side** — *their
strength*, *their weakness*, and *how we win* — then four cards of at most
three one-line bullets each (they sell · their positioning · their customers ·
our read), then their clients as your prospect list.

*How we win* is the one line no competitor's website could ever answer: it is
written from **your brief**, pointed at the weakness above it. If your brief
does not yet say enough for the studio to name a real edge, that line comes
back as a bracketed gap rather than a slogan — brackets are always work still
owed, never an answer. Filling in more of your brief is what turns it into a
sentence you can use.

Reports run before this existed have no three lines and are not re-run for
them; run the report again if you want them.

### Where you stand

Once you hold **two or more** competitor reports, the screen says where you
stand across all of them, above the list they are drawn from: **the one thing
none of them has**, then *where you win* and *where they beat you*, at most
three one-line bullets each.

Four things worth knowing:

- **It reads your reports, not the web.** It is a cross-reading of the three
  lines each report already carries, so it can tell you nothing a report did
  not already find — and it costs no new research.
- **It updates when the set changes**, not on a clock: research another
  competitor, or remove one, and it is drawn again. Add nothing and it stays
  as it was.
- **A competitor you removed is left out of it**, which is the point of
  removing one.
- **Where they beat you is honest on purpose.** A comparison you win
  everywhere is one nobody can act on.

### Likely competitors

The screen opens on **the first page of search results for the phrase your
buyers would type** — a peptides wholesaler lands on *"buy peptides online"* —
and says where you sit on it: *"You are 7th"*, or that you are not on the
first page at all. Every business on that page is one tap from its own
competitor report; a business you have already reported on links that report
instead.

Four things worth knowing about it:

- **It is a live web search, not a tracked Google position.** The number is
  where a result came back on that run. It moves, and it is not measured from
  any one country.
- **Half a first page is usually not a company.** Listicles, forums,
  directories and news pieces are listed where they came back and never
  offered as something to research.
- **The phrase is a guess, and it is yours to change.** *Search a different
  phrase* re-runs the reading on whatever you type.
- **It refreshes itself weekly.** An older reading is drawn straight away and
  a fresh one is fetched behind it, so the screen never makes you wait to be
  told the same ten companies.
The workspace switcher sits at the sidebar's head — click your workspace
name to switch workspaces, set **Appearance** (light / dark / system),
create a client workspace or upload a whole
portfolio of them (agencies), or sign out. An agency workspace is tagged
**(Agency)** in that list with its client workspaces indented under it.
Support sits at the sidebar's foot, next to who you are signed in as.
On a narrow window the sidebar collapses to its icons.

# Pitches — runs, results, editing

## The glance — is this company worth my time?

**Glance** takes about fifteen seconds and answers one question: is this
company worth a full run?

It is on every list of companies the studio shows you — [Leads](/), the
lookalikes on a finished pitch, a Counterprospekt report's client list — and on
[New pitch](/pitch/new). On Leads it leads and **Prospekt** is the word
beside it, because a shelf is for triage and the full run is the purchase you
make after one. A glance goes in your Library like any other reading, and the
shelf stops offering that company — Suggested never proposes work you have
already done, so what is on it is always what you have not looked at yet.

What comes back is one card — a fit score out of 100, the single argument the
case rests on, two or three signals for and against, and the **roles** worth
approaching. It reads the company's own site to do it, capped at two pages and
one search, and the card says how long it took against the fifteen-second
ceiling so you can hold us to it.

**It is kept.** Every finished glance gets a card in the
[Library](/library) — the score, the one thing, the desks it named — marked
**Glance** so it is never mistaken for a pitch. Press the card and you are
back on the glance, with the same presses on it: name the people, write a
piece, or run the full pitch. The card also carries **Run full pitch →** on
its own, because that is the one thing a glance is missing — a finished pitch
carries no button, since pressing it is what opens it. It has its own link,
and it tags and filters like anything else there. Once the full pitch is
finished it takes the glance's place in the list rather than sitting beside
it — one company, one card. Nothing is deleted: the glance keeps its own link
and is still there while the run is out, and if the run fails.

**Two pages buys the front of a business, not all of it.** Where a company
plainly runs more than one line, the card says which one it scored — *"Scored
as a consumer app; it may also have a B2B channel this glance did not read."*
That line is the reason to buy the full run rather than to trust a low score.

**It names roles, never people.** Naming a person needs a source, finding a
source needs searches, and searches are what a fifteen-second answer does not
have. Naming them is the next press.

## Ask for the leads you want

**Describe them and press Find them.** Under the leads on your home screen
there is a box: *"mid-market property managers in the Southeast running class A
and B units"*, *"agencies that already resell Shopify apps"*, *"anyone hiring a
Head of Partnerships this quarter"*. The companies land on the shelf above,
with the same Glance and Prospekt presses every other lead has.

It is the fastest way to two different things:

**The studio has your market slightly wrong.** Rather than correcting it one
company at a time, say what you actually want and get it.

**You want to try something new.** A market you have never worked in, a
one-off idea, a client who asked for something odd. Type it, look at what comes
back, and nothing about your workspace changes.

**Asking never changes your brief.** That is deliberate — most of what people
type here is an experiment, and an experiment that quietly rewrote what the
studio hunts would make the box risky to use for the thing it is best at.

**Ask who moved, not only who fits.** *"Companies that just raised a Series
A"*, *"anyone who opened a UK office this summer"*, *"agencies that changed
their head of growth recently"* — a request that names a time is answered with
companies that moved in one. A card that found something says so on one line —
*"Raised a $40m Series B · 14 Aug"* — and that line opens the page it was read
on. Most companies have not moved and their cards say nothing about when; a
fit score is about whether a company is right, and this is about whether today
is the day.

**We never guess a date.** A move is on the card only when the search read the
event and the day it happened on a page, with the page linked. Nothing older
than six months counts as news.

**Prospekt a company that moved and the move writes the email.** The run is
handed what happened and the day it happened, and inside two months that is the
opening line — why this note is arriving today, in the reader's terms. Older
than that it argues the case and never opens on it: a note congratulating
somebody on something months behind them reads worse than one that never
mentions it. The run checks the move still holds while it reads their pages, and
drops it if what it finds says otherwise.

**A company you typed in gets the same treatment.** The full run looks for a
dated move itself while it reads their pages, so a company you found somewhere
else — New pitch, a portfolio list, a finished pitch's lookalikes — can still
open on why today. Same bar: read on a page, dated, linked, inside six months;
where the run already has a move, the fresher of the two wins.

## Build an agent from a description

**`/agents` — say what you want done, and the studio builds the thing that does
it.** One sentence: *"find agencies in Berlin that already run paid search"*,
*"read Signaliz and tell me who they sell to"*, *"who should I be calling at
Northline?"* The studio picks the door — find leads, lookalikes, a glance, a
pitch, decision-makers, a competitor report — and fills in what that door needs
from your brief.

**The agent is kept.** Next time it is one press, and the list shows when each
one last ran.

**Watch a competitor, and it tells you what to do about each move.** *"Watch
Signaliz every week"* builds a standing watch: the card lists what that company
publicly did since the last look — a launch, a price change, a funding round, a
partnership — each with its date, a link, and one line on what to do about it.
Nothing public since the last watch is a real answer and the card says so. It
reports what a *company* did, never what a person did.

**Say how often and it runs itself.** *"Check Signaliz every Monday"* is a
standing agent: the card shows when it next runs, and **Stop** ends it. Three
agents per workspace may stand at once, and a schedule needs a subscription —
a free workspace keeps the words and the card says so. To add a schedule to an
agent that has none, describe it again with the cadence in the sentence.

**It never invents what you did not say.** *"Watch our biggest rival"* names no
rival, so the card asks which company and nothing else.

**And it says when it cannot.** A sentence the studio has no verb for is
answered as one, not routed to the nearest thing — the agent is kept anyway, so
what you asked for is on the record.

There is nothing else to configure. No model to choose, no tools to switch on,
no prompt to edit: the brief you already wrote is the configuration, which is
why one sentence is enough.

**When it was not an experiment, keep it.** After the results land, one press —
**Always look for these** — puts what you typed on your brief, and every later
search reads it. They are listed on **Your brief** under *What we keep looking
for*, and a cross removes any of them.

**What it will not do:** get past your suppress list, your disqualifiers, or
companies you have already been shown. Asking for something new widens where
the studio looks; it never overrides who you have said no to.

## Is the score wrong? Tell the studio why

**Press the score.** If a company is a better fit than the number says, the
score itself opens one question: *what did we get wrong?* Type a sentence and
press **Re-score**.

Two things happen, and the second one is the point.

**This company is scored again**, in about fifteen seconds, with what you said
taken as given. The new number is earned rather than typed — you do not set the
score, you correct the thing the score was wrong about.

**And the studio learns the part that was about you.** Most corrections contain
two things at once: *"Bozzuto is an excellent fit — we serve class A and B units
**and** luxury operators, we are not limited to lower-income housing."* The
first half is about that one company and stays on its record. The second half is
about **you**, and it goes on your brief — where every future glance, every
company the studio suggests, and every pitch it writes will read it.

That is why a wrong score is worth thirty seconds. Fixing the number helps one
lead; correcting the premise changes what the studio goes looking for.

A green line tells you exactly what was learned, and **Undo** takes it straight
back off if it is not what you meant. Your corrections are listed on **Your
brief**, where you can edit or delete any of them.

**What makes a good correction:** a fact about your company that would still be
useful for a company nobody has mentioned yet. *"We sell to CFOs, not office
managers"* teaches the studio something. *"This one is good"* only fixes this
one.

## Name the people — one press on the glance

**Name the people** sits under the roles on the glance card. One press buys
the searches the glance would not spend: about a minute, capped at four pages
and four searches, and the roles become named people — each with the source
that supports the name, and a LinkedIn link only where a profile was actually
read. A role nobody could be sourced for is then asked of the contact
vendors, who answer with the person who holds it and their profile; where
they have nobody either, the role stays a role, with a null name, because a
guessed name is worse than none. A named person without a profile link is
looked up the same way, so the badge beside the name is their profile
wherever a vendor knows it. People on your workspace's
suppress list are never returned, and a company on it refuses the press the
way it refuses a run. The card prints the timing against the sixty-second
ceiling, the way the glance prints its fifteen.

## What to send — one piece at a time, or everything

Under the glance you decide what to buy. **What to send** offers each piece —
pitch deck, one-pager, cold email, proposal — as its own press: one call,
under 90 seconds, written in your voice with everything your workspace has
taught the studio. Pressing one opens the pitch straight away — the glance's
score and argument are already on it — and the piece lands on its own tab
while you watch. Each further piece is another press on its tab; the pitch
grows as you buy, is saved to your library like any other, and every piece
is editable and shareable the moment it lands. A piece a pitch does not have
yet always shows its press — on staged pitches and on full runs where you
unticked it alike. The compliance check runs on the whole pitch after every
press.

A glance itself is not saved to your library and does not use up anything.
Press **Get the full pitch** on the card and the six-step run starts on the
same company — deeper research, everything written at once.

## Starting a full run

[New pitch](/pitch/new) takes a company name, a bare domain, or both, plus
optionally a point of contact, the partnership motion to argue for, and the
value angle to lead with (the last two come from your workspace's own brief).

Once you have named a company, the **Full pitch** button says how long one
takes — `Full pitch · ~7 min`. That is not an estimate of ours: it is the
middle of your own workspace's finished runs, so it reflects your brief, your
deliverables and how much reading your targets need. It appears once three
runs have finished; before that we do not know yet, and would rather say
nothing than guess. Runs are included in your plan — the minutes are the only
thing a run costs you.

Before anything else, the studio works out **who the company actually is**
from its own website — it opens the site, reads what they sell and to whom,
and rules out same-named businesses. The pitch is then researched, scored
and drafted against that settled identity.

## While it runs

A run takes a few minutes — the button that started it said how many, measured
off your own finished runs — and shows six named stages: understand, research,
score, draft, people, check — with what each stage is actually doing ("2
searches · 9 sources read"; the counts are that step's own work). The stages
are not strictly single-file: the decision-maker search needs only the
confirmed target, so it runs alongside the drafting rather than after it —
**both steps light up at once** while that happens, the foot names both
("Steps 2 & 5 of 6 · BDR + SDR agents"), and step 5 ticks done the moment its
list is ready, even while the drafts are still being written. The drafts
themselves are written **side by side**: each deliverable is its own call —
the same call its press on a finished pitch makes — so the drafting step
takes as long as its slowest piece, not the sum of all of them. A piece that
fails does not fail the run; the finished pitch ships without it, and its
tab holds the press to write it. There is no
percentage bar on purpose: research is one
stage of six, and a long read would sit at 17% looking dead. The clock counts
from when the run started, not from when you opened the screen, so coming back
to a run four minutes in says four minutes. When the draft lands, the terminal
ends with **where the time went** — each step's own clock, from the run's own
record, including what ran in parallel.

**A company the studio already researched is not researched again.** Research
on a target is kept for a month and shared across every workspace on the
deploy, so a rerun — or another workspace pitching the same company — starts
from the settled identity, and the more Prospektor is used the more of your
research is already done. The run says so ("Already researched today — …,
read once for every workspace on Prospektor"), and it caps its remaining
reading to a small, named freshness budget ("Research already settled — capped
at 3 pages · 2 searches"): recent news and anything time-sensitive, never a
re-read of pages it already holds. What crosses is the reading of a public
website and nothing else — the box carries nothing about the workspace that
paid for it, and nothing of your brief, your client or your edits ever reaches
it.

**The steps on the left keep what they found.** The terminal on the right
streams the run as it happens and scrolls; the steps beside it fold each
finished step into a summary that stays for the rest of the run — what your
brief brought to it, who the company turned out to be and which same-named
businesses were ruled out, every page it opened (each one a link you can open
and check) and every search it ran, then each deliverable as it is written. By
the last step that column is the run's own account of itself, and you can read
it without having watched.

Under the six, greyed out, are the three things that come after a finished
pitch — send or share it, prep the call it books, record what happened. They
are signposts to screens you already have, not steps this run takes.

**Each step says who is doing it.** The right-hand column of the rail names the
agent working on that step, and the foot of the run names the one working now.
It is a GTM team, and these are the five:

- **BDR agent** — brings you companies worth pitching. Opens each target's own
  website before anything else and works out who they actually are, not who
  shares their name; scores fit against your brief; suggests the next ones
  worth your time and names the ones it ruled out. *(research, score)*
- **SDR agent** — finds you the way in. Names the decision-makers with a source
  behind every name and a confidence rating on each, and leaves a blank rather
  than inventing one; then finds the warm path through your network. *(people)*
- **AE agent** — writes what you send. Drafts the deck, the one-pager, the
  proposal and the email sequence in your voice, grounded in what has already
  worked for you; preps the call it books. *(draft, and prep afterwards)*
- **Sales Ops agent** — checks the work before you see it. Reads the finished
  draft back against the rules and flags anything that broke one: an invented
  number, a fabricated person, a banned word, a company the research already
  ruled out. It never rewrites your copy — it makes the problem visible next to
  the thing that has it. *(check)*
- **RevOps agent** — remembers what worked. Every outcome you record and every
  edit you save goes into the next run, so run 100 is not run 1. *(learn)*

Two steps carry no agent, and both are deliberate. **Understand the request**
is your own brief read back — you wrote it, so nothing else takes credit for
it. And **send or share it** says *You*: the agents research and draft, and you
send. Nothing here has your relationships, and nothing signs your name.

**The rail's order is the run's order.** A run drafts the deliverables before
it names the decision-makers, so the AE agent appears above the SDR agent on
the rail even though a sales team would introduce them the other way round.
That is the true order the work happens in, and the rail shows it rather than a
tidier one.

Setting up a workspace shows a shorter, three-step rail with no agents on it.
That job is the studio reading *your* site to draft *your* brief — not a pitch,
and it should never look like one.

**You can leave.** The worker runs in the background; [Running](/running)
lists every run in flight with Watch to drop back in. A run nothing has been
heard from in twenty minutes is marked stopped and offers **Dismiss**; a run
still working offers **Stop** (confirmed — it kills real work). There is no
pause.

**Busy moments are retried, and a failure is a fresh start.** The model
provider occasionally has a busy moment; the run says so in its log, backs
off and retries by itself — nothing you entered is lost. A run that fails
anyway says why in one plain sentence and offers two buttons, there and in
*Did not finish*: **Rerun** starts a fresh attempt at the same target with
the same ticked deliverables, and **Share this bug with Prospektor** sends
that run's error and step log to the Prospektor team for analysis — only
when you press it, never on its own.

**Everybody reads every run; your own are yours to manage.** Stopping,
archiving or deleting a run somebody else started — or calling off their
batch — needs the owner or admin role in the workspace. Reading it never
does. (The roles are in [Workspace settings](/help/08-workspace).)

## Beast Mode — a whole list at once

The foot of the New pitch form: upload a CSV or paste one company per line
(`Company name, website` — the website optional) and **Run batch →** queues
every row through the same pipeline. Up to 100 companies per batch, three
running at once, each landing in the Library like any other pitch. The CSV
is parsed in your browser and never uploaded.

**One email at the end, not one per run.** Close the tab — when the last
target lands, the studio emails whoever started the batch: which companies
scored 75% or higher, named, with their own scores and the angle each run
chose, a link straight to each of them, and how many runs landed out of how
many you queued. If nothing cleared 75% the mail says so and names the
closest instead, because that is also the answer. Fifty targets are never
fifty emails, and it is off in one click from the mail itself or in
[Workspace settings](/help/08-workspace).

## Tags — name a list, find it again

You met fifteen companies at an event and ran them. A tag is what makes them
one list afterwards.

**Tag them in the [Library](/library).** The row above your runs carries
**＋ Tag**. Press it, tick the runs that belong together, press **Tag…** and
name the list. One press does all fifteen, and the Library lands on the list
you just made.

**Or name the list before it runs.** The box under Beast Mode's paste area
takes any words you like — `cool event 2026` — and every run in that press
carries it. Leave it empty and the batch behaves exactly as it always did.

**Or one run at a time.** **⋯ → Tag…** on a single card does the same thing
for one. An empty answer clears the tag; there is no separate untag.

Once anything carries one:

- The row grows a chip per list, each counted.
- Pressing a chip narrows the Library to that list; **All** brings the rest back.
- Running says the list's own name instead of "Beast Mode batch".
- Every card names its list on the line under it, beside the date.

The filter is back on **All** next time you open the Library — a filter you
forgot you set empties a screen. Tags are free text, shared with everyone in
the workspace, editable by any of them, never sent anywhere, and deleted with
the run.

**Glances tag the same way.** A glance lands in the Library beside your
pitches, marked **Glance**, so fifteen companies checked the cheap way are one
list like any other.

## Reading the result

A pitch reads as a sequence: Summary → Fit thesis → Signals (for and
against, each rated by recency and recurrence) → Deliverables (deck,
one-pager, cold email, proposal — each block copyable and pencil-editable) →
Decision-makers → Lookalikes. If it is coral, you can click it.

**A run writes the cold email, and leaves the rest to you.** The deck, the
one-pager and the proposal each wait on their own tab with a press button —
one call, under 90 seconds, whenever a pitch turns out to want one. Nothing
is missing and nothing is slower to get; the run simply stops writing three
documents in advance for every company you look at. Decision-makers and
lookalikes always come with the run, because the research call writes them
as it goes.

The Summary is one look, on purpose: the score and name up top, how big
they are, and **The one thing** — the single sentence the pitch rests on.
Everything else the studio worked out — the firm in a paragraph, the four
numbers, what the run drew on from your workspace, and the identity check —
sits behind **The full picture**, one press away on the same tab.

The Fit thesis reads the same way: each bullet of the case and each risk is
one line you can scan, and the objection you will hear comes with a counter
of a few complete sentences you could say back verbatim. Every line ends
properly — the studio rewrites for shortness rather than clipping, so
nothing trails off mid-sentence. The prose version — the argument in full —
sits behind **The full argument**, one press away on the same tab. The
other tabs carry the full detail as they always have.

**The deck is your standing deck, plus one slide.** If the workspace has
written a standing deck ([Your brief](/settings/brief) → *Your standing deck*),
a pitch does not write one: it reuses those slides, drops in a slide about this
company right after the opening one, and fills your prospect's name and business
into the gaps the template left. That is instant and costs no call. A workspace
that has not written one still gets a deck the old way, pressed on its tab.

Three deliverables carry their own shape. The **pitch deck** is real slides:
**Download .pptx** on the deck tab writes a 16:9 file that opens in Keynote,
PowerPoint and Google Slides, one slide per block, in your workspace's own
colours, with the speaker notes on each notes page and the figures' sources
folded in beside them. It is built in your browser, so nothing about the deck
leaves the tab. Edit a slide with its pencil first and the download carries
the edit. Its last slide ends on one quiet line — **Researched by
Prospektor**, the run's source count, the date it ran — the same mark a
shared pitch carries, on the file that gets forwarded furthest. There is no
switch to remove it. The **one-pager** is a value-driven,
print-ready proposal page: your logo and name up top, *why this matters* to
the reader before *why you* are the right one to do it, proof in one-line
points, and one unmissable call to action — Ctrl/Cmd-P turns it into the
page it already looks like. The **proposal** is the formal document you send
once they are interested — scope, commercials and timeline, ready to
forward — and its tab says so, so nobody wonders when to use it.

- **A name appears only when a source supports it** — a page the studio read,
  or a contact vendor's record of who holds the role. A role nobody could be
  named for is asked of the vendors, and stays blank rather than guessed when
  they have nobody at the company in that role. A named person without a
  profile link is looked up the same way; an older pitch gets its profiles
  the next time it is opened.
- **Work emails arrive on their own.** Every named person is looked up with
  two contact vendors, then a routing service that tries eight more, and the
  address lands beside the LinkedIn badge, with what verified it in the tooltip; a catch-all domain is said there too. No
  address means neither vendor had a verified one at the company's own domain —
  an address at a company the person has left is dropped, and so is a shared
  desk like `info@`. Emails are included without a cap; the CSV download
  carries them, a shared link does not. A pitch from before addresses existed
  fills in the first time you open it — give it a few seconds.
- **Phones are one press each, and counted.** A dashed *phone?* beside a
  person's address asks the vendor for their number — by the verified work
  email first, so it is theirs at this company. A number found lands there as
  a tap-to-call link and takes one of your workspace's phone lookups for the
  month; the count left is in the button's tooltip. Nothing found costs
  nothing and reads *no phone*. The CSV carries numbers; a shared link never
  does. If you see no *phone?* at all, phone lookups are not switched on for
  your studio.
- **Bracketed placeholders** in drafts mark what could not be verified.
  They are marked wherever they appear, and the pencil on any block is where
  you fill one in — which also teaches the studio your wording.
- **Find more** under the researched lists queues more research in the
  background — an empty box is a valid instruction ("look again").
- **One specific person** goes in the same box under Decision-makers: a name
  (*Jane Doe*), a LinkedIn profile URL, or either with a role beside it (*Jane
  Doe, CFO*). That person joins the list as you typed them and their work email
  and profile are looked up, the way a run's people are. Someone already listed
  is not added twice. A role on its own (*head of customer operations*) still
  searches for more people.
- **Compliance findings**: the studio still reads its own draft back for
  banned terms and numbers without provenance, and says what it found in the
  run log and the run-ready email. It is a check on the draft, not a screen
  to work through.
- **Who this is**, behind *The full picture* on the Summary, is the studio's answer to the
  question everything else rests on, in one line: *"Identified as Matte PR by
  reading 11 of their own pages · 3 similar companies ruled out."* Under it,
  and open, are the same-named companies it checked and decided were **not**
  your target, each with the reason. The pages themselves are behind *The 11
  pages it read* — one press, and every URL is there with what it learned on
  it. If a company you have never heard of is missing from the ruled-out list
  and its facts are in the profile instead, that is the thing to catch before
  you send anything.
- **Sometimes it says "read 12 days ago", and that is not a shortcut being
  hidden from you.** Working out who a company is means opening their site and
  reading it, and the answer does not change from one week to the next — so
  once any workspace on Prospektor has established it, the reading is kept and
  handed to the next run against that domain instead of being bought again.
  That is why a run can reach the same conclusions in seconds. When the
  reading is not this run's own, the line says when it *was* made, and the
  pages and ruled-out companies behind it are the ones read that day. Nothing
  older than a month is reused — past that the site is read again from
  scratch. If you want a fresh reading sooner than that, say so to support and
  we will clear it for your target.
- **The studio stops looking once it is sure.** Confirming who a company is
  takes a handful of pages, not a hundred: it opens the site, reads the page
  that names the operator, checks that nobody else trades under the name, and
  stops. It spends the full check only where the answer is genuinely in doubt
  — the site would not open, the name you typed is not the name on the site,
  something claims the company has stopped trading, or another business is
  still in the frame. That is why the line above sometimes says four pages and
  sometimes eleven: it is what the answer actually took, not a quota.
- **The highlighted sentences in a draft were written for this company.** Above
  each deliverable a line counts them — *"6 of 21 sentences were written for
  Delvinia"* — and the sentences themselves are marked where you read them.
  A sentence counts when it names something the run established about the
  target: its name, brand, legal entity or domain, one of the decision-makers
  the research named, where it is or how big it is. Its industry does not
  count, because *B2B SaaS* describes the target and everyone it competes
  with. Unmarked is not wrong — your own proof and your own offer belong in the
  draft and are not about the reader. The one to act on is **a draft that names
  nobody**: the studio says so in red, and it means the draft reads as
  something you could send to anyone. On a shared link the recipient sees the
  count and the highlighting, and never that judgement.
- **From your own workspace**, behind *The full picture* on the Summary, says what this run had of
  yours to read: how many recorded outcomes and how many saved edits went
  into the draft. Everything else came from your brief and the live web. A
  run that found no outcomes says so, and offers the door to record one —
  that is the loop that makes a later run better than this one.

## Editing, and what it teaches

The pencil on any deliverable block edits it in place. **Saved edits become
brand-voice examples for future runs** — tone and structure only, never
facts, and facts never cross companies. Editing is the highest-leverage
thing a team does in the studio.

Since 23 Aug 2026 a run chooses those examples **for the company it is
working on** rather than simply taking the three most recent: the ones whose
subject looks most like this target, with at least one example of each
deliverable the run has to write. So a workspace with fifty saved edits
draws on all fifty, a few at a time, instead of on whichever three were
saved last.

Since 25 Aug 2026 the save also records **how long the block was open** before
you pressed it. That is the studio measuring itself, not you: a draft you had to
spend four minutes fixing was a worse draft than one you fixed in twenty
seconds, and that is the only way this product can honestly tell whether a
change to how it writes actually helped. The record is a duration and the kind
of deliverable, with no address on it and nothing you typed; only Prospektor's
operator sees it, as a median across many runs, and nobody in your workspace or
the agency above it ever does. [Privacy](/help/privacy) says it in full, and a
browser sending Global Privacy Control switches it off while your edit saves
exactly as it would have.

A run also carries what your team recorded in [Outcomes](/outcomes) — what
actually won and lost, in their words. The waiting line says so while the
run works: *"Brief loaded, with 4 of your edits as voice references and what
you recorded about 6 companies."* It shapes the judgment, never the copy — a
company from your own outcomes record appearing in a deliverable is flagged by
the compliance check like a banned word is.

## Ask the studio

The last tab of a finished pitch is a conversation about it — where a claim
came from, how to open the first call, what to say when the predicted
objection lands. It answers only from that pitch and your brief, and never
changes the pitch. Each member has their own conversation per pitch; it
survives reloads.

## Print / PDF

Ctrl/Cmd-P prints the deliverable styled with your workspace's own stylesheet
— Save as PDF in the same dialog is the PDF export. A deck prints as a deck:
one slide to a landscape sheet. For a file you can present from and edit, use
**Download .pptx** on the deck tab instead.

There is no Print / PDF button: it duplicated a keystroke your browser already
has, on a screen that reads better without it.
